items.title: The Mathematical Foundations of Intelligence [Professor Yi Ma]
items.summary:
What if everything we think we know about AI understanding is wrong? Is compression the key to intelligence? Or is there something more—a leap from memorization to true abstraction? 

In this fascinating conversation, we sit down with *Professor Yi Ma*—world-renowned expert in deep learning, IEEE/ACM Fellow, and author of the groundbreaking new book *Learning Deep Representations of Data Distributions*. Professor Ma challenges our assumptions about what large language models actually do, reveals why 3D reconstruction isn't the same as understanding, and presents a unified mathematical theory of intelligence built on just two principles: *parsimony* and *self-consistency*.

**SPONSOR MESSAGES START**
—
Prolific - Quality data. From real people. For faster breakthroughs.
https://www.prolific.com/?utm_source=mlst
—
cyber•Fund https://cyber.fund/?utm_source=mlst is a founder-led investment firm accelerating the cybernetic economy
Hiring a SF VC Principal: https://talent.cyber.fund/companies/cyber-fund-2/jobs/57674170-ai-investment-principal#content?utm_source=mlst
Submit investment deck: https://cyber.fund/contact?utm_source=mlst
—
**END**

NOTE: Based on lower retention we have EDITED out 33:45 of the original interview from near the start - philosophical stuff, an extended analogy comparing DNA evolution to AI development, speculation about where theories come from (Platonism, deductive trees), Norbert Wiener's cybernetics history. You can watch the original version on the rescript link or Spotify version. 

Key Insights:

*LLMs Don't Understand—They Memorize*
Language models process text (*already* compressed human knowledge) using the same mechanism we use to learn from raw data. 

*The Illusion of 3D Vision*
Sora and NeRFs etc that can reconstruct 3D scenes still fail miserably at basic spatial reasoning

*"All Roads Lead to Rome"*
Why adding noise is *necessary* for discovering structure.

*Why Gradient Descent Actually Works*
Natural optimization landscapes are surprisingly smooth—a "blessing of dimensionality" 

*Transformers from First Principles*
Transformer architectures can be mathematically derived from compression principles

—

Yi Ma is the inaugural director of the School of Computing and Data Science at Hong Kong University and a visiting professor at UC Berkeley.

items.title: Prompt Debt: The New Trap AI Builders Fall Into
items.summary:
Prompt debt might be the most 2025 kind of technical debt. It’s what happens when AI writes your code… but you never build the mental model behind it.

Shaw Talebi calls it out clearly: LLMs can generate code, architecture, even some of the reasoning. But if you ship something you don’t understand, you’re borrowing against your future self. When things break, when features need to be added, when users show up, you’re stuck with a black box you can’t maintain.

For throwaway tools and single-use dashboards, that’s fine. But for real products, especially SaaS, you need to actually understand what’s happening under the hood. That means not outsourcing the thinking part. Use LLMs as collaborators, not as autopilots. Slow down just enough to form that mental model, then you’ll actually move faster long term with fewer surprises.

That’s how you avoid Prompt debt: stay in the loop, think deeply, build with clarity, and let AI amplify you, not replace you.

I’m Louis-François, PhD dropout, now CTO and co-founder at Towards AI. Follow me for tomorrow’s no BS AI roundup 🚀

items.title: The Weird Skill Combo That Got Me Into Netflix
items.summary:
In episode 947 of the SuperDataScience podcast, Jeffrey Li shares how he was hired at Netflix after multiple previous rejections. He explains that his unique intersection of skills in both advertising (from Spotify) and forecasting made him the perfect candidate when Netflix launched their ads business. Li emphasizes the importance of building niche expertise at the overlap of different industries to differentiate yourself from other candidates.

Additional materials: https://www.superdatascience.com/947

items.title: Future of Science and Technology Q&A (December 12, 2025)
items.summary:
Stephen Wolfram hosts an unscripted Ask Me Anything about the future of science and technology for all ages. Find the playlist of Q&A's here: https://wolfr.am/youtube-sw-qa

Originally livestreamed at: https://twitch.tv/stephen_wolfram

If you missed the original livestream of this episode, feel free to submit a question you would like Stephen to answer in a future Q&A livestream here: https://wolfr.am/12cczmv5J

00:00 Start stream
00:58 SW starts talking
1:12 If alien civilizations evolved their own "computational worldview," how different would their science look from ours?
16:45 If you could ban one buzzword from future science, what would it be?
24:05 Today on the BBC news site there was an article about Google looking for UK experts to find uses for its new quantum chip. Do you think it's difficult to find interesting use cases for quantum computers?
32:33 What do you make of the recurring motif among twentieth-century theoretical physicists leaning in the direction of eastern philosophy?
36:02 If you were building a new house for the future, what would you do or prepare for?
42:43 ​​​​Motion sensors for lights are an upgrade...when you leave, after 15 minutes the lights go off. 
44:12 We have a boiler with in-floor heating throughout...it's the best...no carpet in the house...all stone tile floors are warm always.
48:02 Add a heat sensor as a back up for the lights.
56:28 How can we solve the problem of supplying power to humanoid robots, so that it doesn't have to be plugged in most of the time? Wireless charging, increased battery capacity, more efficient robots...
57:42 Would you trust to have a humanoid robot in your house?
59:11 Maybe a cat robot or a dog would be better.
1:00:49 Painting an interactive thing on a wall makes me think of the Loony Toons Wile E. Coyote painting a fake tunnel on a cliff face. The Road Runner runs right through and the Coyote smacks into it face first.
1:02:10 Would your ideal at-home robot have wheels or legs?
1:04:40 Perhaps people should try making an insect or a small fish robot first, just like nature made them first, and only move on to more advanced creatures later. 
1:10:14 End stream

16:45 If you could ban one buzzword from future science, what would it be?
24:05 Today on the BBC news site there was an article about Google looking for UK experts to find uses for its new quantum chip. Do you think it's difficult to find interesting use cases for quantum computers?
32:33 What do you make of the recurring motif among twentieth-century theoretical physicists leaning in the direction of eastern philosophy?
36:02 If you were building a new house for the future, what would you do or prepare for?
42:43 ​​​​Motion sensors for lights are an upgrade...when you leave, after 15 minutes the lights go off. 
44:12 We have a boiler with in-floor heating throughout...it's the best...no carpet in the house...all stone tile floors are warm always.
48:02 Add a heat sensor as a back up for the lights.
56:28 How can we solve the problem of supplying power to humanoid robots, so that it doesn't have to be plugged in most of the time? Wireless charging, increased battery capacity, more efficient robots...
57:42 Would you trust to have a humanoid robot in your house?
59:11 Maybe a cat robot or a dog would be better.
1:00:49 Painting an interactive thing on a wall makes me think of the Loony Toons Wile E. Coyote painting a fake tunnel on a cliff face. The Road Runner runs right through and the Coyote smacks into it face first.
1:02:10 Would your ideal at-home robot have wheels or legs?
1:04:40 Perhaps people should try making an insect or a small fish robot first, just like nature made them first, and only move on to more advanced creatures later. 
1:10:14 End stream
